summary:
Vigil is an offline health-awareness prototype for astronauts on long missions. It compares each daily reading (sleep, heart rate, HRV, reaction time, mood, stress, cabin CO₂ and radiation dose) with the astronaut’s own baseline, not a population range. When signals move together, such as sleep falling while reaction time slows, Vigil raises one alert with one to three concrete steps, like cutting workload or checking the CO₂ scrubber. The astronaut marks each step Done, or Ignore with a reason, and completed steps change what happens next. A habitat rule separates a shared air problem from an individual one.

Long missions mean delayed or interrupted contact with the ground, so crews must notice and act on health changes themselves. Vigil runs entirely on the device, needs no ground link, and supports awareness and action, not diagnosis. It draws on NASA’s 600 mSv career radiation limit and findings from NASA’s ISS Reaction Self Test study. Crew data in the prototype is simulated.
details:
Vigil is a health-awareness app for astronauts on long missions. Each day it takes the crew member’s readings: sleep, resting heart rate, HRV, reaction time, mood, stress, cabin CO₂ and radiation dose. It compares them with that astronaut’s own last 30 days. A signal is flagged only when it moves the wrong way by both a statistical margin and a minimum percentage, which keeps normal day-to-day variation from raising alerts. Signals that move together become one alert (Watch or Act). A CO₂ rise with shared crew headaches is flagged as a habitat problem, not an individual one. Each alert comes with one to three concrete steps, such as cutting workload by 30% or checking the CO₂ scrubber. The astronaut marks each step Done, or Ignore with a reason. Three screens carry this: Today (status and top alerts), Trends (each signal against a normal-range band) and Actions. All analysis runs on the device with no cloud or ground link.

Benefits

  • Crews can notice and act on changes without waiting for the ground.
  • Alerts are personal, so they fit the individual instead of an average person.
  • Each alert says what to do next.
  • Readings stay on the device.
  • Ignore reasons give feedback for tuning the rules later.

Intended impact
We want crews on missions with limited contact to catch problems early, act on them, and recover faster. In our simulated test case, sleep returned to normal and the alert cleared on day 6 when steps were followed, and on day 9 when they were ignored.

Tools and technology

  • The app is a single web page written in HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with inline SVG charts and no frameworks.
  • We tested the rule engine in Node.js, and tested the screens with Playwright and Chromium.
  • Fonts are Barlow, Barlow Condensed and IBM Plex Mono from Google Fonts.
  • The code and simulated data were generated with Claude, an AI assistant from Anthropic, working from our plan.
  • We used no hardware. All crew data is simulated.
  • NASA sources: the 600 mSv career radiation limit (NASA-STD-3001), NASA’s ISS Reaction Self Test study (Jones et al., 2022), and NASA’s radiation technical brief.

How it is creative

  • The baseline is the astronaut’s own, and it freezes during an episode so a past problem never widens the normal range.
  • It tells a habitat fault apart from an individual health change.
  • It closes the loop from alert to action to recovery. Completed steps change the simulated outcome.
  • A timer mode starts random events so the demo shows how it responds.

What we considered

  • No diagnosis: Vigil gives awareness and action support only.
  • Alert fatigue: the rules produced alerts on 0.7% of normal days across 1,800 simulated days.
  • Time: the interface is meant to be read in about 30 seconds.
  • Accessibility: status uses an icon and text as well as colour.
  • Privacy: the design keeps readings on the device.
  • Validation: the step wording and alert thresholds are placeholders for flight surgeons to review.
  • Limits: the data is simulated.
  • CO₂: NASA removed fixed CO₂ limits in 2022, so we compare CO₂ with the module’s own normal.
dataRefs: NASA Radiation Protection Technical Brief (OCHMO-TB-020 Rev E): 600 mSv career limit under NASA-STD-3001 and the dose figures
NASA Reaction Self Test study of ISS astronauts (Jones et al., Sleep, 2022): ISS sleep and reaction speed
NASA JSC 20584 Rev B, Spacecraft Maximum Allowable Concentrations (checked to confirm NASA removed fixed CO₂ limits)
